proposed_edges.relationship: In “Alfred G. Bailey — Ethnohistorian” (1989), Trigger criticizes Innis for explaining Indigenous participation in the fur trade through universal economic rationality while neglecting particular beliefs and ways of life.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the official Acadiensis PDF, printed p. 5, first paragraph and nn. 7–8 (PDF leaf 3): Innis’s participants become “‘Economic Man’ dressed up in feathers.” Trigger nevertheless credits Innis with recognizing their important role in obtaining furs; n. 8 preserves his acknowledgment of their cultural importance. The note refers back to Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985), pp. 183–184, which were not read. The proposal rests on the 1989 passage, not those unread pages or a claim that Innis simply ignored Indigenous people.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A History of Archaeological Thought, second edition (2006), Trigger contests Kuhnian incommensurability and revolutionary replacement as explanations of archaeological theory.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, pp. 8–9: rival positions are “not incommensurate”; gradual change and recurring positions challenge replacement. He acknowledges Kuhn’s qualifications (pp. 6–7). This reading concerns the 2006 revision; the 1989 first edition is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A History of Archaeological Thought, second edition (2006), Trigger criticizes Foucault’s epistemes for underestimating overlap and inadequately explaining archaeology’s simultaneous theoretical diversity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, pp. 9–10: “Epistemes can contribute little” to explaining concurrent diversity. He allows potential value. Only this introductory passage was checked; no first-edition attribution is made.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing the French translation of Natives and Newcomers (1985; French 1990) in 1992, Dickason endorses Trigger’s warning that excessive reliance on written records distorts Indigenous history, while stressing the limits of archaeological interpretation too.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading: Persée HTML p. 284 identifies the translation and original 1985 publication; p. 285, second paragraph, reads “L’auteur invoque un argument de taille” after summarizing Trigger’s warning. The following sentences stress incomplete records and interpretation problems. Page 285 was read in the project’s previously saved official Persée HTML and visually checked against its saved official image. The Sioui discussion begins in the next paragraph and is excluded. Neither version of Trigger’s book was read; this is a bounded review response, not a personal debt.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A History of Archaeological Thought, second edition (2006), Trigger invokes Carr’s argument that selecting relevant evidence presupposes theory against a model of archaeological data collection preceding explanation.
proposed_edges.map_label: Carr on theory in selecting evidence
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, p. 5: explicitly credits Carr (1967: 3–35). A named methodological resource, not mentorship. Carr’s cited edition and Trigger’s first edition were not read.

Investigated as a distinct influence lead. Trigger’s 1989 p. 16 and n. 53 place his own works within a rationalist-materialist school drawing inspiration from Innis. No additional influence edge is proposed here: the bounded proposal carries his specific criticism, while the broader debt needs closer reading of his unread 1985 discussion. This hold does not negate the materialist inheritance.
